accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England Year 1 writing statement ('using a capital letter for names of people, places, the days of the week, and the personal pronoun I'), English Appendix 2 Year 1 ('capital letters for names and for the personal pronoun I'), the Year 1 spelling list (days of the week) and Common Core L.1.2a ('capitalize dates and names of people'). The proper noun / common noun distinction follows the Oxford English Grammar definitions; pets' names (Rex, Bella, Tom) are proper nouns, and every lab sentence keeps its sentence-start capital so the only change asked for is the name, day or I.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips seen in Year 1 writing samples and the STA exemplification: a small letter on a name (sam, leeds), the lowercase pronoun i (step 4, challenge lowi and lowi2), over-capitalising ordinary nouns that feel important (Dog in the postcard, challenge 'thing'), capitalising every word ('every'), capitalising words that contain the letter i (in, it in step 4, challenge 'inword'), and confusing sunny with Sunday or treating morning as a day name (step 3 prediction and stamp feedback).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagnamecap is about which words are names: a name / not-a-name sort that turns sam into Sam with the capital drawn in a second colour, sentence tiles where only the name accepts a capital, a capital stamp dragged onto day names but refused by sunny, morning and week, a lone-i hunt that refuses in and it, and a postcard where dog must stay small. flagstop (sentence-start capitals and end marks) and flagcaps (forming capital letters) do neither; lab_distinct passed under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each action is tested before any rule is stated in full: dropping park into the name box returns 'park is a kind of thing, not a name. It keeps a small letter', stamping sunny returns 'sunny is about the weather. Sunday is the day name', and tapping in returns 'in has an i inside it, but it is a whole word. Only i on its own, meaning me, is a capital.' Done screens list the fixed sentences with their capitals, so the child sees the pattern across examples.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each have a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: park vs paris (the sort shows only names take capitals), sunny vs sunday (the stamp rejects sunny), and i vs I for 'Mum and ___ went in' (the lone-i step shows I is a capital even mid-sentence). The reveal line repeats the child's own choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Twelve distinct wrong-answer messages across six rotating questions: lowercase I at the start (lowi) and mid-sentence (lowi2), a lowercase person's name (lowname), a lowercase place (place), a pet's name (pet), morning as a day (time), sunny as a day (weather), capitals on every word (every), capitals on ordinary nouns (thing), long words (long), position in the sentence (end) and In inside a sentence (inword).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (Names start with a big letter. It is called a capital letter.), within the family readability limit the validator enforces. Canvas prompts are short (Tap the word that is a name.) on 21-26 px tiles. The adult text uses the precise terms proper noun, common noun and personal pronoun with the statutory wording.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no banned phrases and explanation overlap stayed under 12% against every lesson, including Starting and Ending Sentences (300) and Spaces Between Words (773). Each feedback line names the word and the reason (morning is a time of day, not the name of a day); steps have no warm-up sentences.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots of all six steps in light and dark and a 360 px Android run: the name and not-a-name boxes sit side by side with their 'Big letter' and 'small letter' labels inside the box after the label overflow was fixed, the six day tiles form a 2 x 3 grid of 54 px tiles, sentences wrap onto a second row (My dog is called / rex .), and the postcard text wraps above two 150 x 56 px choice cards. Real touch drags on iPhone 13 sorted sam and dog, stamped Monday, and dropped Monday on the postcard slot.

accessibility.evidence: The walkthrough gate completed all five tasks with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge showed, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme. Every drag or tap has a labelled button below the canvas ('sam: a name', 'Give rex a capital', 'Stamp a capital on friday', 'Write Leeds'), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with every feedback line. Tiles use dark ink on white or pale indigo in both themes.
